title: Chapter 8
content:
Drying off the stray droplets of water, Jakyeong stepped in front of the bathroom mirror.

His body was a map of violent memories. Faint, jagged lines from knife wounds crisscrossed his chest and torso, topped by a rounded scar on his shoulder where a bullet had torn through him years ago. Pulling on the oversized shirt and loose trousers he’d packed, he slipped a pair of glasses onto his face.

On the surface, they were standard black horn-rimmed specs. Concealed within the frame, however, was a micro-camera capable of recording his surroundings and transmitting real-time footage to Wang Han.

Glasses in place, Jakyeong pulled out his phone and dialed Wang Han's encrypted line.

It picked up on the very first ring. Even through the speaker, the sheer anxiety radiating from the other end was palpable.

[Did you make it in alright?]

"Yeah. I'm inside Kang Il-hyun's place."

[Why does your voice sound like you're in a cave?]

"I'm in the bathroom. The house is crawling with CCTV. I can't even make a phone call out in the open."

[Jesus. What's your take on the guy in person?]

Jakyeong recalled the man who had been lounging in his private quarters just moments ago. "He looks even better in person than he does in photos."

[And?]

"And he's ten times more insufferable than I imagined."

[He didn't get to where he is by being a push-over. Don't slip up.]

Jakyeong looked down at his right hand, trace calluses visible across his palm, before catching his own reflection in the mirror. Il-hyun hadn't pressed further when Jakyeong claimed to be an art major. Whether that meant the man swallowed the lie or was simply keeping his cards close, Jakyeong couldn't tell. But the mere fact that suspicion had been seeded was enough to make the air dangerous.

"The inauguration is in three weeks, right?"

[Twenty days, to be exact.]

"I'll keep my head down and stay out of his way until then."

In twenty days, Kang Il-hyun would step up from Executive Director to President and CEO—an absurdly fast ascension for a man his age. The client’s instructions were explicit: put a bullet in Kang Il-hyun at his inauguration, right in front of the crowd.

When a hit called for a public execution over a discreet assassination, it almost always meant a bitter personal vendetta. After meeting Il-hyun today, Jakyeong found he couldn't entirely blame the client.

"The guy really has a talent for grinding your gears," Jakyeong muttered.

[Me?]

"Not you. The target."

[Jakyeong.]

"Yeah?"

Wang Han hesitated, the pause heavy on the line. Jakyeong already knew what was coming next.

[If your gut tells you something's off, pull the plug now. I'll smooth things over with Dmitri.]

Even after sending him off to Korea, Wang Han clearly hadn't made peace with the operation.

"Stop worrying," Jakyeong said quietly. "I'll get the job done and be on the next flight back."

A soft, resigned sigh filtered through the receiver.

"Want me to grab you something from duty-free on my way home?"

[I don't need duty-free crap. Just bring yourself back in one piece. If anything feels wrong, call me instantly.]

"Got it."

Hanging up, Jakyeong took one last look at his attire before stepping out of the bathroom. He took care to move naturally, ignoring the camera mounted near the ceiling. Unzipping his suitcase, he unpacked his clothes, stowed them away in the closet, and climbed onto the bed.

He opened a thick book—one Wang Han had forced into his luggage to help him look the part of a studious young heir. Reading had always been Jakyeong's least favorite chore, and the block of text on the page blurred almost immediately. He flipped through a few pages on pure discipline before slipping into a rhythmic cycle of nodding off and snapping back awake.

Beyond the long, dimly lit corridor, several private dining chambers sat tucked away in the exclusive establishment. Guided by an attendant, Il-hyun arrived at the innermost room.

Sliding the wooden door open, he found three men already seated inside. They were senior board members of Haewon Group—veterans who had helped the Chairman, Kang Hoon, transition their underground operations into a legitimate corporate empire. Unsurprisingly, all three were staunch supporters of the eldest son, Kang Tae-han, for the succession.

"My apologies for keeping you waiting," Il-hyun said, offering a crisp, polite bow before taking his seat.

The three executives, who had half-risen from their cushions, settled back down with visibly tense expressions. They had accepted Il-hyun's invitation out of necessity, but a private dinner with him was the last place any of them wanted to be.

Ignoring the suffocating atmosphere, Il-hyun casually wiped his hands with the warm towel provided by the server.

"I must admit, Executive Director Kang, I was surprised by your invitation," Director Kim, the most influential of the three, remarked dryly.

"Nothing out of the ordinary, Director Kim," Il-hyun replied smoothly. "It simply occurred to me that it had been far too long since I last treated my seniors to a proper meal."

The three men exchanged discreet, wary glances. Prior to arriving, they had pledged an unwritten pact: under no circumstances would they back Il-hyun for the succession. Tae-han’s maternal grandfather was a former member of the National Assembly who, despite his retirement, still wielded significant political pull that benefited the company immensely.

Il-hyun, on the other hand, had no maternal backing to speak of. His mother had been wed to Kang Hoon almost by force—sold off to settle her own father's staggering debts. Consumed by resentment, she spent her married years drowning in alcohol before hanging herself, leaving her young children behind.

Course after course arrived as the conversation touched on routine corporate affairs. Il-hyun poured wine into their glasses with practiced grace, and as the alcohol took effect, the stiff air gradually thawed.

A quiet knock at the sliding door broke the rhythm.

Park Tae-soo stepped into the room, carrying a leather briefcase. Unzipping it, he pulled out a document and set it down.

Il-hyun slid the paper across the table toward the three executives.

"What is this?" Director Kim asked, picking it up.

"A consent form for relocating the safe," Il-hyun said softly.

Director Kim scanned the lines of fine print. Chairman Kang Hoon and four key directors maintained an off-the-books vault reserved for laundering and distributing black-market capital. Recently, however, prosecution investigators had begun sniffing around the operation, forcing an emergency relocation of the assets.

The executives were already aware of the situation, making its sudden appearance at a dinner table puzzling. Furthermore, the document required four signatures. The fourth name on the line—Director Yoon Kyung-hwan—was absent from the table entirely.

"Why bring this out now?" Director Kim frowned. "Yoon isn't even here."

Director Yoon had been completely unreachble since the previous evening.

"Has anyone managed to get ahold of him yet?" one of the other executives asked.

"Not a word. What on earth is he doing at a time like this?"

"Probably holed up in a hotel with some girl," another sneered. "Leopards don't change their spots."

Listening quietly to their chatter, Il-hyun let out a silent, chilling smile. "You don't need to worry about Director Yoon's signature."

He shot Tae-soo a subtle look. Tae-soo reached back into his briefcase, pulled out a small wooden box, and set it on the table.

The three executives leaned in slightly, eyeing the box with mild curiosity. Tae-soo lifted the lid, and Il-hyun reached inside.

"Ah—!"

Director Kim and the two men beside him recoiled, their faces contorting in horror.

What Il-hyun held in his hand was a severed human finger. The dried blood around the severed joint was dark and crusty.

"Dear God! You—!"

"Director Yoon was unable to attend in person," Il-hyun said smoothly, "so I brought his representation."

"You... you monster!"

"Tae-soo. The ink pad."

Tae-soo produced a small tin of red stamp ink and opened it. Il-hyun pressed the severed digit into the thick ink, completely indifferent to the blood drained from the faces around him.

"It's the right thumb, correct?"

"Yes, sir," Tae-soo confirmed.

Il-hyun pressed the inked thumb firmly onto the signature line beside Director Yoon's printed name. Done, he dropped the severed finger directly into his wine glass with a soft plop, then picked up a damp towel to wipe his hands clean.

The three directors sat frozen, staring in sheer terror at the severed digit floating in the red wine.

Director Kim was the first to find his voice, his tone sharp with outrage. "What is the meaning of this insolence?! How dare you bring such a sickening stunt to this table!"

Il-hyun met his gaze directly. "Does this look like a stunt to you, Director Kim?"

Cornered by that pit-viper stare, Director Kim slammed his hand on the table and stood up. "I'm leaving. I'm going straight to the Chairman about this!"

Il-hyun reached into his glass, fished out the finger, dropped it onto a clean side plate, and drained the remaining wine in a single gulp.

Director Kim's eye twitched uncontrollably.

Setting the empty glass down with a quiet clink, Il-hyun offered a look of mild, mocking regret. "It came to my attention that Director Yoon has been quietly financing a few organ harvesting rings."

Director Kim stiffened visible. Organ harvesting.

Il-hyun leaned forward, locking his gaze onto Kim's eyes. While the other two directors looked genuinely oblivious, Kim's guilty reaction was unmistakable. The old man had cut himself a piece of that pie too.

"I have no idea what you're talking about," Kim stammered, trying to hold his composure.

Old bastard. Still playing dumb.

"I certainly hope that's true," Il-hyun murmured, his tone dripping with fake affection. "If I had to take your fingers too, Director Kim... imagine how brokenhearted my father would be. Right?"

"You disrespectful brat!"

As the standoff intensified, the remaining two directors sat paralyzed, desperately trying to calculate which side of the war offered them a higher chance of survival.

Breaking the silence, Il-hyun picked up his suit jacket from the back of his chair and stood up. He didn't miss the subtle trembling in Director Kim's clenched fists.

For all his illegal dealings, Chairman Kang Hoon maintained a few strict, unyielding boundaries—and human organ trafficking was top of the list. Yoon had crossed that red line to raise off-the-books capital for a private casino project on the southern coast.

"I'll leave the rest of the meal to the three of you," Il-hyun smiled pleasantly. "The uninvited guest will take his leave."

Watching that smug, unbothered smile, Director Kim finally snapped, shouting at Il-hyun's back: "Do you think this makes you the heir?! The Chairman will never give you the company! Don't even dream of it!"

Il-hyun maintained his polite smile, offered the three men a crisp bow, and stepped out into the hallway.

The moment the door slid shut behind him, the smile vanished entirely from his face. Inside the room, an absolute, terrified silence reigned. He didn't need to look through the door to know those old snakes were frantically running numbers in their heads.

Yet one thing was certain: none of them would dare make a move against him now. Not when they knew their own fingers could be floating in a wine glass next.

Translator's Notes (A/N):

Organ Harvesting Slang (통나무 장사): Literally translated as "log trading," tong-namu jang-sa is Korean underworld slang for human organ trafficking, where victims or bodies are dehumanized and referred to as "logs" (tong-namu).
Seal / Thumbprint Stamp (지장): In Korean legal and official documents, a thumbprint dipped in red ink (in-ju) serves as a legally binding signature (ji-jang), often used alongside or in place of a personal seal (do-jang). Il-hyun using the victim's actual thumb enforces a terrifyingly literal, binding agreement.
